position_in_era.historical_role: Mutation of the Sabbath riff-first contract into a neoclassical harmonic vocabulary: Ritchie Blackmore's four-note riff (G–Bb–C, G–Bb–Db–C) uses perfect fourths and a minor third rather than a tritone, generating weight through interval stacking rather than satanic dissonance. The riff is now the most recognisable in rock history — proof that the riff-first principle could produce pop accessibility as well as dread.

narrative_slots.production_facts: Recorded December 1971 at the Montreux Casino and Grand Hotel, Montreux, Switzerland, after the casino burned down during a Frank Zappa concert (the fire becomes the song's lyric). Produced by Deep Purple. Blackmore played the riff on guitar; Roger Glover doubles it on bass. The riff uses two strings only, played without distortion — the simplicity is deliberate, contrasting with Purple's usual keyboard-heavy sound.
narrative_slots.member_dynamics: Blackmore conceived the riff; Ian Gillan wrote the lyrics documenting the Montreux fire in real time. Jon Lord's organ is absent from the verse riff, giving Blackmore's guitar and Glover's bass the weight-carrying role that Iommi and Butler share in Sabbath. The riff creates the song; the organ and vocal are secondary.
narrative_slots.instrumentation_details: Blackmore: Fender Stratocaster (unusual for him — chosen for the riff's clean attack); Glover: bass doubling the riff; Lord: Hammond organ (chorus only); Gillan: vocal; Paice: drums. The riff in G minor uses the interval sequence P4–m3 rather than Sabbath's tritone.
narrative_slots.cultural_venue: Released as a single (US, 1973); reached #4 US. The riff became the first thing most guitarists learn to play — its cultural penetration has made it both the most famous mutation of the Sabbath riff principle and a marker of beginner guitar culture. The song's narrative (fire, emergency, outdoor recording) became a rock mythology document.
narrative_slots.release_circumstances: Machine Head was recorded in a Rolling Stones Mobile Studio parked outside the Grand Hotel. The album reached #1 UK. The song was not initially released as a UK single — its chart success came from US radio airplay two years after the album.
